_about: College batch 9: the last freshman scenes (COL_034, 035), all nine sophomore drafts (COL_044, 051, 054, 060, 061, 066-069), then junior COL_070 (opened by COL_066) and COL_077.

scenarios.title: Winter Conditioning
scenarios.text: Winter conditioning starts at 5:30 a.m., in the dark, in the snow. Three teammates have already started skipping and signing each other in on the attendance sheet, and they've offered to sign you in too.

choices.label: Let them sign you in
choices.result: You sleep in twice. The third time, the strength coach checks the sheet against the door cameras, and every name on it gets a phone call home and a meeting with {coach}.

choices.label: Show up every morning
choices.result: You're there at 5:30 every day for six weeks. By February, you're the one the freshmen follow across the parking lot.

choices.label: Show up and bring them
choices.result: You start knocking on their doors at 5:10. Two of them start coming. The third stops answering the door.

choices.label: Add your own plan on top
choices.result: You show up every morning and add the plan you've kept since high school in the evenings. It's a lot, and by spring your leg feels like somebody else's.
choices.lock_text: having built your own training plan before

scenarios.title: Spring Kicking Competition
scenarios.text: Spring practice opens with a kicking competition for next season. The veteran kicker is graduating, the job is open, and {coach} will chart every kick for three weeks.

choices.label: Treat it like a job interview
choices.result: You show up early, chart your own kicks next to {coach}'s chart and ask for feedback after every session. By the end, the coach is asking you what you see.

choices.label: Kick loose and have fun with it
choices.result: You treat it like a backyard contest and trash-talk the other kickers all spring. It keeps you relaxed, and it doesn't make {coach} smile.

choices.label: Help the other kickers too
choices.result: You share your warmup with the other kickers in the competition, even the one chasing your spot. The room gets better, and so do they.

scenarios.title: The High School Tape
scenarios.text: {coach} rewatches your old recruiting tape and stops on one clip: a long kick in perfect conditions with the distance marker cropped out. 'Tell me about this one,' the coach says.

choices.label: Tell the truth about the clip
choices.result: You say it was a practice kick, wind at your back, and the crop was your idea. {coach} nods slowly and says the honest answer is worth more than the clip.

choices.label: Shrug and change the subject
choices.result: You say it was a long time ago and ask about this week's practice plan. {coach} lets it go, and doesn't forget it.

choices.label: Stop defending it
choices.result: You defended that clip once to a high school coach. This time you don't. You tell {coach} the whole thing, including the defending.
choices.lock_text: having defended that clip in high school

choices.label: Say you fixed it years ago
choices.result: You tell {coach} you caught it in high school and sent the corrected version to every coach. The coach checks the files, finds it, and smiles.
choices.lock_text: having corrected that video in high school

scenarios.title: The Visit Home
scenarios.text: You go home for the first time in months. Your old room is a storage closet now, {parent} has a new routine you don't know, and {best_friend} keeps talking about people you've never met.

choices.label: Ask about the new stuff
choices.result: You ask {parent} about his new routine and {best_friend} about the new friends, and you mean it. By the end of the week, you're in some of the stories.

choices.label: Bring back the old routine
choices.result: You talk {best_friend} into the old diner, the old field and the old jokes. It's good, and it's a little like visiting a museum.

choices.label: Cut the trip short
choices.result: You go back to campus two days early and spend them in the weight room. It's easier than feeling like a guest at home.

scenarios.title: {parent} Loses His Job
scenarios.text: {parent} finally tells you: the cut hours turned into a layoff. He says he'll figure it out. You have a little NIL money in the bank and a semester of books still to buy.

choices.label: Send money home
choices.result: You send most of what you have and don't tell anyone on the team. {parent} calls to argue, then to say thank you.

choices.label: Keep it for school
choices.result: You talk it through with {parent}, and he insists: keep it for books and rent, so he doesn't have to worry about you too. You do, and you call every Sunday.

choices.label: Send half, keep half
choices.result: You split it down the middle. It doesn't solve either problem, and it helps both a little.

scenarios.title: The Summer Plan
scenarios.text: Summer is three choices: summer classes to get ahead, a circuit of kicking camps, or a job back home that pays real money.

choices.label: Summer classes
choices.result: You stay on campus and take two classes. It's hot and quiet, and you start the fall a semester ahead.

choices.label: The kicking camp circuit
choices.result: You drive to four camps in six weeks and kick in front of coaches who've never heard of you. Your leg's never been more tired, or better.

choices.label: The job back home
choices.result: You work at the warehouse and kick in the park at night. You come back with money in the bank and calluses on the wrong body part.

choices.label: Job by day, your plan by night
choices.result: You take the job back home and run your own training plan every evening. It's exhausting, and it's the most complete summer you've had.
choices.lock_text: having built your own training plan before

scenarios.title: The Holder Who Wants Out
scenarios.text: {holder} wants to stop holding and focus on winning a starting job in the secondary. It means a new holder for you in the middle of the season.

choices.label: Back {holder}'s decision
choices.result: You tell {holder} to go get the job and offer to help break in the replacement. It costs you two weeks of awkward holds.

choices.label: Ask {holder} to stay through the season
choices.result: You ask {holder} to hold until the season ends and chase the job in spring. {holder} agrees, a little reluctantly.

choices.label: Find a way to do both
choices.result: You go to {coach} with a plan: {holder} holds on game days and spends the rest of the week with the secondary. The coach is skeptical, then says yes.

scenarios.title: The Head Coach Is Fired
scenarios.text: The head coach is fired the morning after the last game. Staff jobs are up in the air, {coach} may not be back, and half the roster is checking the transfer portal.

choices.label: Stay and say so
choices.result: You tell {coach} and the athletic director you're staying, no matter who they hire. It's a bet on yourself and on this place.

choices.label: Look at your options
choices.result: You put your name in a few group chats and take a couple of calls, just to know what's out there. Nothing's decided, and the program notices.

choices.label: Wait and see who they hire
choices.result: You decide to wait for the new staff before deciding anything. It's sensible, and a lot of anxious weeks.

scenarios.title: The Fundraiser Nobody Wants to Run
scenarios.text: The children's hospital asks the team to run a kick-a-thon fundraiser: pledges per field goal in practice, kids on the sideline. Someone has to organize it, and nobody's volunteering.

choices.label: Run it yourself
choices.result: You spend three weeks on sponsors, permits and pledge sheets. The kick-a-thon raises more than the hospital asked for, and two of the kids wear your number.

choices.label: Share it with the specialists
choices.result: You split the work with the punter and the snapper. It's smaller, and it gets done.

choices.label: Let someone else take it
choices.result: You say you're too busy this month, which is true. The event happens without you, and you watch it on someone else's phone.

choices.label: Bring in your old volunteer contacts
choices.result: You call the people you volunteered with back home, who know exactly how to run one of these. It's the best-run event the team's ever had.
choices.lock_text: having volunteered in your community before

scenarios.title: Spring Break
scenarios.text: Spring break, and teammates are going to the beach. Offseason lifts are optional that week, and so, it seems, are the team's rules.

choices.label: Go, and keep your rules
choices.result: You go, lift at the hotel gym every morning and are in bed before anything gets loud. You come back tan, rested and with nothing to explain.

choices.label: Stay on campus
choices.result: You stay and use the empty facility all week. It's quiet, a little lonely, and productive.

choices.label: Go all in
choices.result: You go to every party and stay out every night. On Thursday, the police break one up, and your name ends up on a list that gets back to {coach} before you do.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Camp Coach
scenarios.text: A private kicking coach who has sent players to the pros offers you a spot in his elite summer group, but only if you drop the school's summer program that {coach} runs.

choices.label: Join the private group
choices.result: You join. The drills are brilliant, the price is high, and {coach} takes it personally.

choices.label: Stay with the school program
choices.result: You thank him and stay. The program is less flashy, and {coach} gives you more reps than ever.

choices.label: Ask {coach} to make it work
choices.result: You ask {coach} whether you could do the private group's first two weeks and then come back. It takes two meetings, and the coach agrees.

choices.label: Check his record first
choices.result: You call two of his former players before deciding. One loved him; one says he ruins hips. You stay with {coach} and borrow his best drill.
choices.lock_text: having checked out a trainer before trusting him

scenarios.title: The New Head Coach
scenarios.text: The new head coach starts with a team meeting and a new rulebook: phones in a basket, no hats indoors, every player at breakfast. He says he's already heard about every player on the roster.

choices.label: Buy in from day one
choices.result: You're at breakfast early every day for a month. The new staff notices, and so do the players who were waiting to see which way the room would go.

choices.label: Ask him what he heard about you
choices.result: You knock on his door and ask, straight out, what he's heard about you. He tells you, and it's fairer than you expected.

choices.label: Keep your head down
choices.result: You follow the new rules and say nothing. It's safe. It also means the new staff learns about you from other people.

scenarios.title: The Transfer Kicker
scenarios.text: A kicker with a big resume transfers in from another school, and the coaches love his leg. {coach} says the job is open again.

choices.label: Compete for it
choices.result: You out-prepare everyone: film, sleep, charts. You don't say a word about the transfer, good or bad, and {coach} notices that too.

choices.label: Welcome him in
choices.result: You show the transfer around and invite him to the specialists' dinner. It's strange to help the person chasing your job, and the room respects it.

choices.label: Make his life harder
choices.result: You 'forget' to tell him about schedule changes and move his ball bag twice. He figures it out in a week, and so does {coach}.

choices.label: Do what you did in high school
choices.result: You helped a rival for your job once and it made you both better. You split warmups with the transfer and push each other every day.
choices.lock_text: having helped a teammate who was competing with you
